The optimal PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF scaffold demonstrated compressive strength of 12 MPa, porosity 
of 72%, swelling of 1860%, and biodegradation of 43% over 21 days, while the PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF 
scaffold exhibited a compressive strength of 8.1 MPa and porosity of 79%. Both scaffolds showed good 
biomineralization in SBF and a favorable cell viability rate (OD) in MTT toxicity tests, with an OD of 
1.483 and 1.451 for PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF and PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF scaffolds, respectively. These findings 
suggest that the PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF nanocomposite scaffold is a promising candidate for bone tissue 
engineering applications. By adding hydroxyapatite and magnetic clay modified with graphene oxide 
to the polymer scaffold, the mechanical properties of the scaffold are increased, appropriate porosity 
and swelling values are obtained, and desirable cell viability is achieved.

Failure  of  tissues  and  organs  due  to  damage,  congenital  disabilities,  and  aging  is  becoming  the  main  issue 
of  human  body  health  all  over  the  world.  Bones  are  one  of  the  strongest  and  primary  tissues  of  the  body, 
maintaining  the  surrounding  soft  tissues1.  Regarding  synthetic  scaffolds  that  promote  bone  tissue  repair,  the 
dual role of bone tissue engineering (BTE) scaffolds in interacting with the extracellular matrix and providing 
load-bearing capacity is a challenge. This research aims to investigate the use and processing of several materials 
and  hierarchical  architectures  to  simulate  the  structure  of  natural  bone  tissues  so  that  they  may  function  as 
bioactive artificial scaffolds2. It is widely believed that designing and preparing new tissues is one of the most

A new strategy for repairing bones has emerged that is based on tissue engineering. As a result of its use of 
biomaterial scaffolds along with cells and growth factors, it can induce the formation of new bone tissues while 
reducing the risks associated with autologous bone grafts4. Bone tissue is a composite of approximately 70% 
nano-hydroxyapatite and 30% collagen. Wet collagen and the accumulation of mineral crystals penetrate each 
other and form a mineral fiber on a scale of several hundred nanometers. The primary role of bone is to provide 
a  structural  framework  and  mechanical  strength,  regulate  blood  pH,  and  maintain  calcium  and  phosphate 
levels for metabolic processes5. It is desirable to design a biocompatible composite that can mimic the natural 
extracellular bone matrix and accelerate new bone regeneration6. If the dispersed phase used in the composite is 
nanoparticles, the composite material will be a nanocomposite. Natural bone is an example of a nanocomposite 
composed of two major phases, organic and inorganic, at the nanoscale7. Polymer-based nanocomposites are 
attractive  due  to  their  ability  to  create  porous  architectures  and  biodegradability.  The  ease  of  manipulating 
structures  with  precise  tuning  of  physicochemical  properties  is  an  advantage  of  polymer  nanocomposites 
for  tissue  engineering  applications  such  as  dental,  bone,  and  neural  engineering8.  Nanocomposites  made  of 
polymeric materials and additives are potential materials for constructing bone scaffolds9.

Polymers for making hydrogels include natural and synthetic polymers. Natural polymers are mainly natural 
components  that  prepare  scaffolds  with  high  biocompatibility,  biodegradability,  and  natural  cell  adhesion. 
Recently, synthetic polymers have been widely used to make bone tissue engineering scaffolds because they have 
high mechanical properties and long life. Carboxymethyl cellulose is a biocompatible and biodegradable anionic 
polymer that can create a strong ionic cross-link in the scaffold10 and increase the biochemical characteristics 
of porosity, swelling, and degradation. Cellulose is mainly used for various biomedical applications11. Among 
natural polysaccharides, alginate biopolymer is also widely used as a biomaterial for bone tissue engineering. 
Alginate is one of the most well-known substances, and it has the property of forming a suitable scaffold that can 
be useful for the treatment of organ failure and loss. Alginate consists of guluronic acid and mannuronic acid 
and is used in tissue engineering due to its biocompatibility, non-toxicity, abundance, and low price12. Alginate 
hydrogels can increase minimal protein absorption due to their hydrophilic property13. Sodium alginate is anionic 
and can be dissolved in water. Hydroxyl groups can cause strong interactions between sodium alginate and other 
polymers through hydrogen bonding14. Alginate benefits osteoblast growth due to its functional groups, such 
as hydroxyl and carboxyl, and increases the efficiency of implant substrates. Due to its high degradation rate in 
cell culture, its use in biomedical applications is limited. To improve alginate’s biocompatibility and mechanical 
properties, its combination with synthetic polymers and clay minerals was investigated15. Given the disadvantages 
of  natural  polymers,  such  as  poor  solubility  in  common  solvents,  their  low  mechanical  properties,  and  poor 
stability in physiological environments, There have been numerous studies conducted on the physicochemical 
properties of composite polymers, which have proven to be effective in overcoming the disadvantages of natural 
polymers16. Blending polymers is a potential method for improving mechanical flexibility17. Polyvinyl alcohol 
is a hydrophilic semi-crystalline synthetic biopolymer containing many hydroxyl groups, and it can also form 
hydrogen  bonds  with  free  water  molecules18.  Polyvinyl  alcohol  is  biocompatible  and  has  high  mechanical 
strength, low toxicity, large surface area, and good chemical stability; in a clinical setting, its use is possible to 
construct membranes, repair tissues, and construct biomaterials16. By synergistically combining the bioactive 
properties of nanoparticles and the properties of polymers, composite materials create scaffolds that provide an 
optimal environment for cell proliferation, differentiation, and cell adhesion19. Various natural and synthetic 
fillers  are  used  as  strengthening  agents  to  improve  polymer  scaffolds’  mechanical  properties  and  bioactivity. 
Clay is considered one of the mineral fillers that will enhance the biological and mechanical properties of the 
scaffold  significantly,  and  it  has  already  been  studied  in  bone  cement  processing20.  Clay  can  be  essential  in 
bone regeneration and repair, increasing osteoblast differentiation and apatite deposition20. Also, the graphene 
oxide filler is highly compatible with the polymer matrix due to the attendance of polar groups on the surface 
of  this  material. The  high  exceptional  area  ratio  and  antibacterial  properties  make  GO  a  promising  material 
for developing bone tissue’s antimicrobial and antiviral surface21. GO is exfoliated from graphite and contains 
epoxide, carboxylic, and carbonyl ketone groups in its structural plane. Graphene and graphene-based materials 
have been investigated in various fields, such as bioimaging, biosensors, cancer treatment, drug delivery, and 
tissue engineering. Unique properties such as thermal conductivity, mechanical strength, high surface area, ease 
of operation, flexibility, biocompatibility, and antibacterial activity make it suitable for biological applications. 
GO has osteoconductive and osteoinductive ability to regulate osteoblast differentiation22,23. Also, this substance 
can force stem cells to undergo osteogenic differentiation even without adding a growth factor24. Hydroxyapatite 
contains basic elements such as calcium and phosphate, essential for bone growth. HAp particles increase cell 
proliferation and adhesion and improve bone tissue conduction23. Hydroxyapatite has unique properties, such 
as excellent biocompatibility and low toxicity25. Combining ceramic filler and polymer matrix in one material 
produces  composites  with  polymer  plasticity  and  calcium  phosphate  bioactivity26.  Scaffolds  containing  HAp 
have stronger mechanical properties and higher cell proliferation than scaffolds containing TCP, which gives 
them a better function in bone regeneration in the early stages27. Nanoparticle content can be used to modify the 
properties of polymer nanocomposites28. Various magnetic nanoparticles have been developed recently for use 
in biological applications. Among these nanoparticles, iron oxide nanoparticles (Fe3O4) have biocompatibility 
and  good  performance  for  medical  applications.  Many  researchers  have  shown  that  the  magnetic  properties 
of Fe3O4 nanoparticles make it an ideal material for cell isolation and drug delivery, which also increases the 
effect of bone induction. Several studies have shown that integrating Fe3O4 nanoparticles with polymer fibers 
solves the compaction problem and improves their stability in biological applications29. The research fabricates 
nanocomposite  scaffolds  using  CMC,  Alg,  PVA,  magnetic  clay  nanoparticles  modified  with  graphene  oxide 
(CGF), and natural hydroxyapatite (HAp) to enhance mechanical properties. Characterization involved XRD, 
FT-IR, TGA, and SEM analyses, assessing porosity, swelling, degradation, and biomineralization, and the MTT

synthetic polymer and an additive, each of which can only be used to improve one property. In this study, two 
biopolymers are compared in terms of the composition of scaffolds. Two additives are also used: HAp can be 
used to improve biomineralization, and CGF is a combination of several materials that can give many favorable 
properties to the polymer composite for use as a polymer scaffold.

Having  the  required  mechanical  properties  is  one  of  the  most  important  properties  that  bone  tissue 
replacement  scaffolds  must  possess.  In  addition  to  having  the  required  mechanical  properties,  the  scaffolds 
should possess other characteristics required by bone tissue, such as porosity, biocompatibility, swelling, and 
non-toxicity. A significant aspect of the research is that in addition to increasing compressive strength, attention 
has been paid to maintaining the required porosity of the bone tissue. A combination of graphene oxide, clay, 
hydroxyapatite, and the magnetic material Fe3O4 has been used in this research as a new material. As a result of 
the combination of graphene oxide with clay, the compressive strength of the scaffold was increased significantly, 
and the presence of HAp led to an increase in biomineralization of the scaffold, whereas Fe3O4 had a positive 
effect on the viability of the cells. The properties of natural bone differ significantly based on its type. For example, 
the compressive strength of cancellous bone ranges from 2 to 20 MPa. As a result, it is important to consider 
the scaffold’s mechanical properties when designing scaffolds for bone reconstruction and fracture healing to 
ensure a successful outcome30. It has been found that the scaffold that was prepared in this study has compressive 
strength within the acceptable range for cancellous bone. It is important to  emphasize that the porosity of a 
hydrogel is a significant factor that profoundly affects the fate of bone cells31. A series of interconnected pores 
in this hydrogel facilitate the migration of cells, the permeability of nutrients, the removal of waste materials, 
and the penetration of blood vessels and nerves32. The porosity of cancellous bone ranges from 30 to 70%33. The 
porosity of the scaffolds prepared for this study is within an appropriate range for cancellous bone scaffolds. 
The prepared scaffolds had appropriate degradation rates because replacing the manufactured tissue with the 
original tissue would have to occur within a proper biodegradation range. Also, they exhibited a high degree of 
cell viability.

Materials and methods
Materials
Sodium alginate (Na-Alg) polymer with a molecular weight of 12,000–40,000 Da from Sigma Aldrich, sodium 
carboxymethyl  cellulose  with  a  molecular  weight  of  70,000  g/mol  and  a  deacetylation  degree  of  90%  from 
Samchun, Korea, and polyvinyl alcohol with a molecular weight of 72,000 g/mol and a hydrolysis degree of 95% 
from  Merck  were  used  in  this  study.  Potassium  hydrogen  phosphate  (KH2PO4),  sodium  hydroxide  (NaOH), 
and  25%  glutaraldehyde  as  cross-linkers  were  obtained  from  Merck.  The  acids  used  in  this  study,  including 
hydrochloric  acid  (HCl)  37%,  phosphoric  acid  (H3PO4),  acetic  acid  (CH3COOH)  100%,  and  sulfuric  acid 
(H2SO4) 98%, were all obtained from Merck. Cloisite 30B clay was organically modified to be the clay used in 
the study, obtained from Southern Clay Company. K2HPO4.3H2O, KCl, NaCl, Na2SO4, MgCl2.6H2O, NaHCO3, 
CaCl2.2H2O, and TRIS salts prepared simulated body fluid purchased from Merck. Iron (II) chloride, Iron (III) 
chloride, KMnO4, and H2O2 were used to modify clay.

Synthesis of graphene oxide
To prepare graphene oxide using the modified Hummer method. First, 3 g of graphite powder was added to 
the H2SO4/H3PO4 mixture (40:360 ml), and then 18 g of KMnO4 was added and stirred at 50 °C for 14 h with 
100 rpm by a magnetic stirrer. The temperature of the resulting mixture was reduced to 25 °C, and then 30% 
H2O2 was added to it, making the mixture light brown and stirred for 20 min. A centrifuge was used to separate 
the mixture, and several washes were done with distilled water to reach a neutral pH. In a vacuum oven, 24 h of 
drying time was spent at 70 °C on the synthesized graphene oxide34. Graphene oxide was synthesized in black 
and in powder form.

Preparation of magnetically modified clay
To prepare magnetically modified clay, 1 g of synthesized graphene oxide (GO) was sonicated in 100 mL of water 
for 35 min, while 2 g of Cloisite 30B clay was sonicated in 100 mL of water for 20 min. A solution of iron(III) 
chloride and iron(II) chloride in a 1:2 molar ratio was then added to the GO-clay mixture, which was heated 
and stirred at 90 °C for 20 min. The resulting mixture was gradually combined with a 4 M sodium hydroxide 
solution and stirred for 50 min. Finally, the modified clay was separated from the solution, washed several times 
with distilled water, and baked at 105 °C for 4 h.

Preparation of natural hydroxyapatite (HAp) powder
The  chicken  femur  was  cleaned  entirely  of  meat  and  remaining  materials  to  prepare  natural  hydroxyapatite 
powder  and  then  boiled  for  45  min  in  boiling  water.  The  cleaned  bones  were  placed  in  a  furnace  for  3  h  at 
900 °C with a nitrogen atmosphere. After the set time, the bones are removed from the oven, cooled to room 
temperature,  and  then  powdered  once  they  are  at  room  temperature.  The  production  efficiency  of  natural 
hydroxyapatite powder is 58%, and the product is white35.

Preparation of nanocomposite scaffold
The  nanocomposite  scaffolds  were  prepared  using  natural  polymer  materials,  PVA,  hydroxyapatite  extracted 
from  natural  bone,  and  modified  clay  using  a  simple  mixing  method.  For  the  preparation  of  the  scaffold,  a 
solution of 2 wt. in the first step. % of a natural polymer in distilled water was prepared by dissolving the polymer 
in the water and stirring the solution until the polymer was fully dissolved. It was also possible to prepare a

Characterization of scaffolds
Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) study
To examine the functional and chemical properties of HAp, Fe3O4, GO, clay, Cloisite 30B/GO/Fe3O4, Alg, CMC, 
PVA, and their interactions, we performed FTIR analysis on the prepared nanocomposite scaffolds. Infrared 
spectra of the samples, mixed with KBr powder, were recorded using a Bruker Tensor 27 spectrophotometer 
(Germany). This FTIR instrument offers a measurement resolution of 0.1 cm⁻1, and its readings are based on 
absorbance.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) study
XRD  analysis  evaluated  the  crystallinity  of  PVA,  CMC,  Alg,  HAp,  clay,  and  C30B/GO/Fe3O4  samples  and 
the  prepared  nanocomposite  scaffolds.  The  analysis  was  performed  using  a  Krisallofex  D500  diffractometer 
(Siemens, Germany), which employed Cu-Kα radiation at 25 mA, operating at 40 kV, and scanned over a range 
of 4–80°. The device had a scan step of 0.05° and a measurement accuracy of 0.04 deg/sec.

Morphology study of scaffold samples by SEM analysis
The  scaffolds  were  prepared  by  freeze-drying  and  then  coated  with  a  thin  layer  of  gold  after  being  cut  into 
thin sheets. Once the samples were positioned in the microscope, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images 
(MIRA3, TESCAN, Brno, Czech Republic) were used to examine the morphology of the scaffolds. Furthermore, 
the  presence  and  distribution  of  phosphorus  and  calcium  elements  within  the  nanocomposite  scaffold  were 
analyzed using energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX)  mapping. A voltage  of 30  kV was applied to the SEM device. 
Also, to image the amount of cell culture by SEM, uniform pieces of the scaffolds were cut and immersed in 70% 
ethanol solution for 30 min for sterilization. In the next step, the samples were washed three times with PBS to 
remove excess ethanol and then transferred to a 6-well cell culture plate. A cell plate with a density of 50,000 cells 
per cell plate was then used to culture the MSCs on scaffolds. As a final step, the samples were cultured in an 
FBS medium with 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 10% DMEM in an incubator for 72 h. They were incubated 
for 72 h at 37 °C. After this time, the supernatant of all the wells of the 6-well plate was removed, and after 
washing with PBS, they were fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde for 20 min. After removing the fixative solution,

Mechanical properties study
The  mechanical  properties  of  the  scaffold  samples  were  evaluated  by  measuring  the  compressive  strength 
prepared by freeze-drying. To assess the material’s compressive strength, cylinder samples measuring 12 mm in 
height and 6 mm in diameter were cut. During a compression test, a force with 0.5 mm per minute speed and 
power of 25 kN was used to test the material’s compressive strength at 25 °C. A universal machine model was 
used to carry out mechanical tests, Al-7000-Taiwand. Three samples of each scaffold were prepared to perform 
the compressive strength test, and all three samples were tested. Their average compressive strength was reported 
as the compressive strength of the polymer scaffold. The error value was 0.1 MPa.

Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) study
The  thermal  stability  of  the  polymer  raw  materials  and  nanocomposite  scaffolds  was  assessed  using  TGA.  A 
thermogravimetric  analyzer  (TGA-PL,  TGA  1500,  Canada)  was  employed  for  this  analysis,  conducted  in  a 
nitrogen atmosphere within the 25–600°C temperature range.

Investigation of scaffold biomineralization using simulated body fluid (SBF)
The performance of the scaffold bone graft was assessed using simulated body fluid (SBF), which was prepared 
following  established  protocols  with  chemical  reagents.  SBF  is  essential  for  examining  the  formation  of 
biomaterials on polymer scaffolds. To prepare the solution, 1000 mL of SBF was made by adding 700 mL of 
deionized water into a plastic container in a water bath. It is recommended to cover the container with either 
a glass or plastic lid while stirring; for the process to be successful, the solution should be kept at a consistent 
temperature of 36.5 °C throughout. Adding the ingredients in order is essential; once each ingredient is dissolved 
completely, the next one should be added, and so on. As soon as the ingredients were added, hydrochloric acid 
was used in the amount of 0–5 ml with an additive solution to achieve a pH of 7.4 in the resulting solution after 
adding the ingredients. A total of 1000 mL of solution was prepared by adding water to a flask and shaking it 
at 20 °C to reach the desired volume. The solution was then transferred to a polyethylene container and stored 
in a refrigerator at 5–10 °C. Scaffold samples were immersed in the SBF solution and incubated at 37 °C for 14 
days. After incubation, the samples were removed, rinsed with distilled water, and dried using the freeze-drying 
method. Finally, EDX and SEM techniques were employed to evaluate the biomineralization capability of the 
scaffold samples38.

Eventually, we must continue using PBS to remove any remaining ethanol from the system and transfer it to a

Recently, synthetic polymers have been widely used to make bone tissue engineering scaffolds because they have 
high mechanical properties and long life. Carboxymethyl cellulose is a biocompatible and biodegradable anionic 
polymer that can create a strong ionic cross-link in the scaffold10 and increase the biochemical characteristics 
of porosity, swelling, and degradation. Cellulose is mainly used for various biomedical applications11. Among 
natural polysaccharides, alginate biopolymer is also widely used as a biomaterial for bone tissue engineering. 
Alginate is one of the most well-known substances, and it has the property of forming a suitable scaffold that can 
be useful for the treatment of organ failure and loss. Alginate consists of guluronic acid and mannuronic acid 
and is used in tissue engineering due to its biocompatibility, non-toxicity, abundance, and low price12. Alginate 
hydrogels can increase minimal protein absorption due to their hydrophilic property13. Sodium alginate is anionic 
and can be dissolved in water. Hydroxyl groups can cause strong interactions between sodium alginate and other 
polymers through hydrogen bonding14. Alginate benefits osteoblast growth due to its functional groups, such 
as hydroxyl and carboxyl, and increases the efficiency of implant substrates. Due to its high degradation rate in 
cell culture, its use in biomedical applications is limited. To improve alginate’s biocompatibility and mechanical 
properties, its combination with synthetic polymers and clay minerals was investigated15. Given the disadvantages 
of  natural  polymers,  such  as  poor  solubility  in  common  solvents,  their  low  mechanical  properties,  and  poor 
stability in physiological environments, There have been numerous studies conducted on the physicochemical 
properties of composite polymers, which have proven to be effective in overcoming the disadvantages of natural 
polymers16. Blending polymers is a potential method for improving mechanical flexibility17. Polyvinyl alcohol 
is a hydrophilic semi-crystalline synthetic biopolymer containing many hydroxyl groups, and it can also form 
hydrogen  bonds  with  free  water  molecules18.  Polyvinyl  alcohol  is  biocompatible  and  has  high  mechanical 
strength, low toxicity, large surface area, and good chemical stability; in a clinical setting, its use is possible to 
construct membranes, repair tissues, and construct biomaterials16. By synergistically combining the bioactive 
properties of nanoparticles and the properties of polymers, composite materials create scaffolds that provide an 
optimal environment for cell proliferation, differentiation, and cell adhesion19. Various natural and synthetic 
fillers  are  used  as  strengthening  agents  to  improve  polymer  scaffolds’  mechanical  properties  and  bioactivity. 
Clay is considered one of the mineral fillers that will enhance the biological and mechanical properties of the 
scaffold  significantly,  and  it  has  already  been  studied  in  bone  cement  processing20.  Clay  can  be  essential  in 
bone regeneration and repair, increasing osteoblast differentiation and apatite deposition20. Also, the graphene 
oxide filler is highly compatible with the polymer matrix due to the attendance of polar groups on the surface 
of  this  material. The  high  exceptional  area  ratio  and  antibacterial  properties  make  GO  a  promising  material 
for developing bone tissue’s antimicrobial and antiviral surface21. GO is exfoliated from graphite and contains 
epoxide, carboxylic, and carbonyl ketone groups in its structural plane. Graphene and graphene-based materials 
have been investigated in various fields, such as bioimaging, biosensors, cancer treatment, drug delivery, and 
tissue engineering. Unique properties such as thermal conductivity, mechanical strength, high surface area, ease 
of operation, flexibility, biocompatibility, and antibacterial activity make it suitable for biological applications. 
GO has osteoconductive and osteoinductive ability to regulate osteoblast differentiation22,23. Also, this substance 
can force stem cells to undergo osteogenic differentiation even without adding a growth factor24. Hydroxyapatite 
contains basic elements such as calcium and phosphate, essential for bone growth. HAp particles increase cell 
proliferation and adhesion and improve bone tissue conduction23. Hydroxyapatite has unique properties, such 
as excellent biocompatibility and low toxicity25. Combining ceramic filler and polymer matrix in one material 
produces  composites  with  polymer  plasticity  and  calcium  phosphate  bioactivity26.  Scaffolds  containing  HAp 
have stronger mechanical properties and higher cell proliferation than scaffolds containing TCP, which gives 
them a better function in bone regeneration in the early stages27. Nanoparticle content can be used to modify the 
properties of polymer nanocomposites28. Various magnetic nanoparticles have been developed recently for use 
in biological applications. Among these nanoparticles, iron oxide nanoparticles (Fe3O4) have biocompatibility 
and  good  performance  for  medical  applications.  Many  researchers  have  shown  that  the  magnetic  properties 
of Fe3O4 nanoparticles make it an ideal material for cell isolation and drug delivery, which also increases the 
effect of bone induction. Several studies have shown that integrating Fe3O4 nanoparticles with polymer fibers 
solves the compaction problem and improves their stability in biological applications29. The research fabricates 
nanocomposite  scaffolds  using  CMC,  Alg,  PVA,  magnetic  clay  nanoparticles  modified  with  graphene  oxide 
(CGF), and natural hydroxyapatite (HAp) to enhance mechanical properties. Characterization involved XRD,

synthetic polymer and an additive, each of which can only be used to improve one property. In this study, two 
biopolymers are compared in terms of the composition of scaffolds. Two additives are also used: HAp can be 
used to improve biomineralization, and CGF is a combination of several materials that can give many favorable 
properties to the polymer composite for use as a polymer scaffold.

Having  the  required  mechanical  properties  is  one  of  the  most  important  properties  that  bone  tissue 
replacement  scaffolds  must  possess.  In  addition  to  having  the  required  mechanical  properties,  the  scaffolds 
should possess other characteristics required by bone tissue, such as porosity, biocompatibility, swelling, and 
non-toxicity. A significant aspect of the research is that in addition to increasing compressive strength, attention 
has been paid to maintaining the required porosity of the bone tissue. A combination of graphene oxide, clay, 
hydroxyapatite, and the magnetic material Fe3O4 has been used in this research as a new material. As a result of 
the combination of graphene oxide with clay, the compressive strength of the scaffold was increased significantly, 
and the presence of HAp led to an increase in biomineralization of the scaffold, whereas Fe3O4 had a positive 
effect on the viability of the cells. The properties of natural bone differ significantly based on its type. For example, 
the compressive strength of cancellous bone ranges from 2 to 20 MPa. As a result, it is important to consider 
the scaffold’s mechanical properties when designing scaffolds for bone reconstruction and fracture healing to 
ensure a successful outcome30. It has been found that the scaffold that was prepared in this study has compressive 
strength within the acceptable range for cancellous bone. It is important to  emphasize that the porosity of a 
hydrogel is a significant factor that profoundly affects the fate of bone cells31. A series of interconnected pores 
in this hydrogel facilitate the migration of cells, the permeability of nutrients, the removal of waste materials, 
and the penetration of blood vessels and nerves32. The porosity of cancellous bone ranges from 30 to 70%33. The 
porosity of the scaffolds prepared for this study is within an appropriate range for cancellous bone scaffolds. 
The prepared scaffolds had appropriate degradation rates because replacing the manufactured tissue with the 
original tissue would have to occur within a proper biodegradation range. Also, they exhibited a high degree of 
cell viability.

Materials
Sodium alginate (Na-Alg) polymer with a molecular weight of 12,000–40,000 Da from Sigma Aldrich, sodium 
carboxymethyl  cellulose  with  a  molecular  weight  of  70,000  g/mol  and  a  deacetylation  degree  of  90%  from 
Samchun, Korea, and polyvinyl alcohol with a molecular weight of 72,000 g/mol and a hydrolysis degree of 95% 
from  Merck  were  used  in  this  study.  Potassium  hydrogen  phosphate  (KH2PO4),  sodium  hydroxide  (NaOH), 
and  25%  glutaraldehyde  as  cross-linkers  were  obtained  from  Merck.  The  acids  used  in  this  study,  including 
hydrochloric  acid  (HCl)  37%,  phosphoric  acid  (H3PO4),  acetic  acid  (CH3COOH)  100%,  and  sulfuric  acid 
(H2SO4) 98%, were all obtained from Merck. Cloisite 30B clay was organically modified to be the clay used in 
the study, obtained from Southern Clay Company. K2HPO4.3H2O, KCl, NaCl, Na2SO4, MgCl2.6H2O, NaHCO3, 
CaCl2.2H2O, and TRIS salts prepared simulated body fluid purchased from Merck. Iron (II) chloride, Iron (III) 
chloride, KMnO4, and H2O2 were used to modify clay.

Synthesis of graphene oxide
To prepare graphene oxide using the modified Hummer method. First, 3 g of graphite powder was added to 
the H2SO4/H3PO4 mixture (40:360 ml), and then 18 g of KMnO4 was added and stirred at 50 °C for 14 h with 
100 rpm by a magnetic stirrer. The temperature of the resulting mixture was reduced to 25 °C, and then 30% 
H2O2 was added to it, making the mixture light brown and stirred for 20 min. A centrifuge was used to separate 
the mixture, and several washes were done with distilled water to reach a neutral pH. In a vacuum oven, 24 h of 
drying time was spent at 70 °C on the synthesized graphene oxide34. Graphene oxide was synthesized in black 
and in powder form.

Preparation of magnetically modified clay
To prepare magnetically modified clay, 1 g of synthesized graphene oxide (GO) was sonicated in 100 mL of water 
for 35 min, while 2 g of Cloisite 30B clay was sonicated in 100 mL of water for 20 min. A solution of iron(III) 
chloride and iron(II) chloride in a 1:2 molar ratio was then added to the GO-clay mixture, which was heated 
and stirred at 90 °C for 20 min. The resulting mixture was gradually combined with a 4 M sodium hydroxide 
solution and stirred for 50 min. Finally, the modified clay was separated from the solution, washed several times 
with distilled water, and baked at 105 °C for 4 h.

Preparation of natural hydroxyapatite (HAp) powder
The  chicken  femur  was  cleaned  entirely  of  meat  and  remaining  materials  to  prepare  natural  hydroxyapatite 
powder  and  then  boiled  for  45  min  in  boiling  water.  The  cleaned  bones  were  placed  in  a  furnace  for  3  h  at 
900 °C with a nitrogen atmosphere. After the set time, the bones are removed from the oven, cooled to room 
temperature,  and  then  powdered  once  they  are  at  room  temperature.  The  production  efficiency  of  natural 
hydroxyapatite powder is 58%, and the product is white35.

absorbance.

Fabrication of biodegradable 
nanocomposite scaffolds with 
hydroxyapatite, magnetic clay, 
and graphene oxide for bone tissue 
engineering

Akram Babakhani1, Seyed Jamaleddin Peighambardoust1, Maryam Ghahremani-Nasab2,4 
& Naeimeh Sadat Peighambardoust3

Bone tissue engineering offers an alternative approach to producing scaffolds using biodegradable 
materials. The extracellular matrix of bone tissue comprises collagen and hydroxyapatite so that 
regenerated scaffolds can be a combination of polymeric materials and hydroxyapatite. Additives 
are also used to improve the properties and bring the properties of the regenerated scaffold closer to 
bone tissue. This study focuses on developing nanocomposite scaffolds composed of natural polymers 
carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and alginate (Alg), combined with the synthetic polymer polyvinyl 
alcohol (PVA) as the polymer matrix. The mechanical properties of these biopolymers were enhanced 
using magnetic clay nanoparticles modified with graphene oxide (CGF) and natural hydroxyapatite 
(HAp). Modified clay was synthesized by adding graphene oxide (via the modified Hummer’s 
method), clay, and Fe3O4 nanoparticles. Nanocomposite scaffolds were prepared using the freeze-
drying process, incorporating 10 wt. % HAp and 2 wt. % CGF as optimal additives. Comprehensive 
characterization, including XRD, FT-IR, TGA, SEM, and analysis of porosity, swelling, degradation, 
and biomineralization, confirmed the formation of a porous polymer matrix with favorable properties. 
The optimal PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF scaffold demonstrated compressive strength of 12 MPa, porosity 
of 72%, swelling of 1860%, and biodegradation of 43% over 21 days, while the PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF 
scaffold exhibited a compressive strength of 8.1 MPa and porosity of 79%. Both scaffolds showed good 
biomineralization in SBF and a favorable cell viability rate (OD) in MTT toxicity tests, with an OD of 
1.483 and 1.451 for PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF and PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF scaffolds, respectively. These findings 
suggest that the PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF nanocomposite scaffold is a promising candidate for bone tissue 
engineering applications. By adding hydroxyapatite and magnetic clay modified with graphene oxide 
to the polymer scaffold, the mechanical properties of the scaffold are increased, appropriate porosity 
and swelling values are obtained, and desirable cell viability is achieved.

Keywords  Magnetic nanoclay, Hydroxyapatite, Nanocomposite scaffold, Graphene oxide, Bone tissue 
engineering

Failure  of  tissues  and  organs  due  to  damage,  congenital  disabilities,  and  aging  is  becoming  the  main  issue 
of  human  body  health  all  over  the  world.  Bones  are  one  of  the  strongest  and  primary  tissues  of  the  body, 
maintaining  the  surrounding  soft  tissues1.  Regarding  synthetic  scaffolds  that  promote  bone  tissue  repair,  the 
dual role of bone tissue engineering (BTE) scaffolds in interacting with the extracellular matrix and providing 
load-bearing capacity is a challenge. This research aims to investigate the use and processing of several materials 
and  hierarchical  architectures  to  simulate  the  structure  of  natural  bone  tissues  so  that  they  may  function  as 
bioactive artificial scaffolds2. It is widely believed that designing and preparing new tissues is one of the most

effective and efficient ways that tissue engineering can accelerate bone regeneration during the healing process3. 
A new strategy for repairing bones has emerged that is based on tissue engineering. As a result of its use of 
biomaterial scaffolds along with cells and growth factors, it can induce the formation of new bone tissues while 
reducing the risks associated with autologous bone grafts4. Bone tissue is a composite of approximately 70% 
nano-hydroxyapatite and 30% collagen. Wet collagen and the accumulation of mineral crystals penetrate each 
other and form a mineral fiber on a scale of several hundred nanometers. The primary role of bone is to provide 
a  structural  framework  and  mechanical  strength,  regulate  blood  pH,  and  maintain  calcium  and  phosphate 
levels for metabolic processes5. It is desirable to design a biocompatible composite that can mimic the natural 
extracellular bone matrix and accelerate new bone regeneration6. If the dispersed phase used in the composite is 
nanoparticles, the composite material will be a nanocomposite. Natural bone is an example of a nanocomposite 
composed of two major phases, organic and inorganic, at the nanoscale7. Polymer-based nanocomposites are 
attractive  due  to  their  ability  to  create  porous  architectures  and  biodegradability.  The  ease  of  manipulating 
structures  with  precise  tuning  of  physicochemical  properties  is  an  advantage  of  polymer  nanocomposites 
for  tissue  engineering  applications  such  as  dental,  bone,  and  neural  engineering8.  Nanocomposites  made  of 
polymeric materials and additives are potential materials for constructing bone scaffolds9.

Polymers for making hydrogels include natural and synthetic polymers. Natural polymers are mainly natural 
components  that  prepare  scaffolds  with  high  biocompatibility,  biodegradability,  and  natural  cell  adhesion. 
Recently, synthetic polymers have been widely used to make bone tissue engineering scaffolds because they have 
high mechanical properties and long life. Carboxymethyl cellulose is a biocompatible and biodegradable anionic 
polymer that can create a strong ionic cross-link in the scaffold10 and increase the biochemical characteristics 
of porosity, swelling, and degradation. Cellulose is mainly used for various biomedical applications11. Among 
natural polysaccharides, alginate biopolymer is also widely used as a biomaterial for bone tissue engineering. 
Alginate is one of the most well-known substances, and it has the property of forming a suitable scaffold that can 
be useful for the treatment of organ failure and loss. Alginate consists of guluronic acid and mannuronic acid 
and is used in tissue engineering due to its biocompatibility, non-toxicity, abundance, and low price12. Alginate 
hydrogels can increase minimal protein absorption due to their hydrophilic property13. Sodium alginate is anionic 
and can be dissolved in water. Hydroxyl groups can cause strong interactions between sodium alginate and other 
polymers through hydrogen bonding14. Alginate benefits osteoblast growth due to its functional groups, such 
as hydroxyl and carboxyl, and increases the efficiency of implant substrates. Due to its high degradation rate in 
cell culture, its use in biomedical applications is limited. To improve alginate’s biocompatibility and mechanical 
properties, its combination with synthetic polymers and clay minerals was investigated15. Given the disadvantages 
of  natural  polymers,  such  as  poor  solubility  in  common  solvents,  their  low  mechanical  properties,  and  poor 
stability in physiological environments, There have been numerous studies conducted on the physicochemical 
properties of composite polymers, which have proven to be effective in overcoming the disadvantages of natural 
polymers16. Blending polymers is a potential method for improving mechanical flexibility17. Polyvinyl alcohol 
is a hydrophilic semi-crystalline synthetic biopolymer containing many hydroxyl groups, and it can also form 
hydrogen  bonds  with  free  water  molecules18.  Polyvinyl  alcohol  is  biocompatible  and  has  high  mechanical 
strength, low toxicity, large surface area, and good chemical stability; in a clinical setting, its use is possible to 
construct membranes, repair tissues, and construct biomaterials16. By synergistically combining the bioactive 
properties of nanoparticles and the properties of polymers, composite materials create scaffolds that provide an 
optimal environment for cell proliferation, differentiation, and cell adhesion19. Various natural and synthetic 
fillers  are  used  as  strengthening  agents  to  improve  polymer  scaffolds’  mechanical  properties  and  bioactivity. 
Clay is considered one of the mineral fillers that will enhance the biological and mechanical properties of the 
scaffold  significantly,  and  it  has  already  been  studied  in  bone  cement  processing20.  Clay  can  be  essential  in 
bone regeneration and repair, increasing osteoblast differentiation and apatite deposition20. Also, the graphene 
oxide filler is highly compatible with the polymer matrix due to the attendance of polar groups on the surface 
of  this  material. The  high  exceptional  area  ratio  and  antibacterial  properties  make  GO  a  promising  material 
for developing bone tissue’s antimicrobial and antiviral surface21. GO is exfoliated from graphite and contains 
epoxide, carboxylic, and carbonyl ketone groups in its structural plane. Graphene and graphene-based materials 
have been investigated in various fields, such as bioimaging, biosensors, cancer treatment, drug delivery, and 
tissue engineering. Unique properties such as thermal conductivity, mechanical strength, high surface area, ease 
of operation, flexibility, biocompatibility, and antibacterial activity make it suitable for biological applications. 
GO has osteoconductive and osteoinductive ability to regulate osteoblast differentiation22,23. Also, this substance 
can force stem cells to undergo osteogenic differentiation even without adding a growth factor24. Hydroxyapatite 
contains basic elements such as calcium and phosphate, essential for bone growth. HAp particles increase cell 
proliferation and adhesion and improve bone tissue conduction23. Hydroxyapatite has unique properties, such 
as excellent biocompatibility and low toxicity25. Combining ceramic filler and polymer matrix in one material 
produces  composites  with  polymer  plasticity  and  calcium  phosphate  bioactivity26.  Scaffolds  containing  HAp 
have stronger mechanical properties and higher cell proliferation than scaffolds containing TCP, which gives 
them a better function in bone regeneration in the early stages27. Nanoparticle content can be used to modify the 
properties of polymer nanocomposites28. Various magnetic nanoparticles have been developed recently for use 
in biological applications. Among these nanoparticles, iron oxide nanoparticles (Fe3O4) have biocompatibility 
and  good  performance  for  medical  applications.  Many  researchers  have  shown  that  the  magnetic  properties 
of Fe3O4 nanoparticles make it an ideal material for cell isolation and drug delivery, which also increases the 
effect of bone induction. Several studies have shown that integrating Fe3O4 nanoparticles with polymer fibers 
solves the compaction problem and improves their stability in biological applications29. The research fabricates 
nanocomposite  scaffolds  using  CMC,  Alg,  PVA,  magnetic  clay  nanoparticles  modified  with  graphene  oxide 
(CGF), and natural hydroxyapatite (HAp) to enhance mechanical properties. Characterization involved XRD, 
FT-IR, TGA, and SEM analyses, assessing porosity, swelling, degradation, and biomineralization, and the MTT

| https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-07270-5

test  evaluated  cell  viability.  In  bone  tissue  research,  the  composites  studied  mainly  combine  a  natural  and 
synthetic polymer and an additive, each of which can only be used to improve one property. In this study, two 
biopolymers are compared in terms of the composition of scaffolds. Two additives are also used: HAp can be 
used to improve biomineralization, and CGF is a combination of several materials that can give many favorable 
properties to the polymer composite for use as a polymer scaffold.

Having  the  required  mechanical  properties  is  one  of  the  most  important  properties  that  bone  tissue 
replacement  scaffolds  must  possess.  In  addition  to  having  the  required  mechanical  properties,  the  scaffolds 
should possess other characteristics required by bone tissue, such as porosity, biocompatibility, swelling, and 
non-toxicity. A significant aspect of the research is that in addition to increasing compressive strength, attention 
has been paid to maintaining the required porosity of the bone tissue. A combination of graphene oxide, clay, 
hydroxyapatite, and the magnetic material Fe3O4 has been used in this research as a new material. As a result of 
the combination of graphene oxide with clay, the compressive strength of the scaffold was increased significantly, 
and the presence of HAp led to an increase in biomineralization of the scaffold, whereas Fe3O4 had a positive 
effect on the viability of the cells. The properties of natural bone differ significantly based on its type. For example, 
the compressive strength of cancellous bone ranges from 2 to 20 MPa. As a result, it is important to consider 
the scaffold’s mechanical properties when designing scaffolds for bone reconstruction and fracture healing to 
ensure a successful outcome30. It has been found that the scaffold that was prepared in this study has compressive 
strength within the acceptable range for cancellous bone. It is important to  emphasize that the porosity of a 
hydrogel is a significant factor that profoundly affects the fate of bone cells31. A series of interconnected pores 
in this hydrogel facilitate the migration of cells, the permeability of nutrients, the removal of waste materials, 
and the penetration of blood vessels and nerves32. The porosity of cancellous bone ranges from 30 to 70%33. The 
porosity of the scaffolds prepared for this study is within an appropriate range for cancellous bone scaffolds. 
The prepared scaffolds had appropriate degradation rates because replacing the manufactured tissue with the 
original tissue would have to occur within a proper biodegradation range. Also, they exhibited a high degree of 
cell viability.

Materials and methods
Materials
Sodium alginate (Na-Alg) polymer with a molecular weight of 12,000–40,000 Da from Sigma Aldrich, sodium 
carboxymethyl  cellulose  with  a  molecular  weight  of  70,000  g/mol  and  a  deacetylation  degree  of  90%  from 
Samchun, Korea, and polyvinyl alcohol with a molecular weight of 72,000 g/mol and a hydrolysis degree of 95% 
from  Merck  were  used  in  this  study.  Potassium  hydrogen  phosphate  (KH2PO4),  sodium  hydroxide  (NaOH), 
and  25%  glutaraldehyde  as  cross-linkers  were  obtained  from  Merck.  The  acids  used  in  this  study,  including 
hydrochloric  acid  (HCl)  37%,  phosphoric  acid  (H3PO4),  acetic  acid  (CH3COOH)  100%,  and  sulfuric  acid 
(H2SO4) 98%, were all obtained from Merck. Cloisite 30B clay was organically modified to be the clay used in 
the study, obtained from Southern Clay Company. K2HPO4.3H2O, KCl, NaCl, Na2SO4, MgCl2.6H2O, NaHCO3, 
CaCl2.2H2O, and TRIS salts prepared simulated body fluid purchased from Merck. Iron (II) chloride, Iron (III) 
chloride, KMnO4, and H2O2 were used to modify clay.

Synthesis of graphene oxide
To prepare graphene oxide using the modified Hummer method. First, 3 g of graphite powder was added to 
the H2SO4/H3PO4 mixture (40:360 ml), and then 18 g of KMnO4 was added and stirred at 50 °C for 14 h with 
100 rpm by a magnetic stirrer. The temperature of the resulting mixture was reduced to 25 °C, and then 30% 
H2O2 was added to it, making the mixture light brown and stirred for 20 min. A centrifuge was used to separate 
the mixture, and several washes were done with distilled water to reach a neutral pH. In a vacuum oven, 24 h of 
drying time was spent at 70 °C on the synthesized graphene oxide34. Graphene oxide was synthesized in black 
and in powder form.

Preparation of magnetically modified clay
To prepare magnetically modified clay, 1 g of synthesized graphene oxide (GO) was sonicated in 100 mL of water 
for 35 min, while 2 g of Cloisite 30B clay was sonicated in 100 mL of water for 20 min. A solution of iron(III) 
chloride and iron(II) chloride in a 1:2 molar ratio was then added to the GO-clay mixture, which was heated 
and stirred at 90 °C for 20 min. The resulting mixture was gradually combined with a 4 M sodium hydroxide 
solution and stirred for 50 min. Finally, the modified clay was separated from the solution, washed several times 
with distilled water, and baked at 105 °C for 4 h.

Preparation of natural hydroxyapatite (HAp) powder
The  chicken  femur  was  cleaned  entirely  of  meat  and  remaining  materials  to  prepare  natural  hydroxyapatite 
powder  and  then  boiled  for  45  min  in  boiling  water.  The  cleaned  bones  were  placed  in  a  furnace  for  3  h  at 
900 °C with a nitrogen atmosphere. After the set time, the bones are removed from the oven, cooled to room 
temperature,  and  then  powdered  once  they  are  at  room  temperature.  The  production  efficiency  of  natural 
hydroxyapatite powder is 58%, and the product is white35.

Preparation of nanocomposite scaffold
The  nanocomposite  scaffolds  were  prepared  using  natural  polymer  materials,  PVA,  hydroxyapatite  extracted 
from  natural  bone,  and  modified  clay  using  a  simple  mixing  method.  For  the  preparation  of  the  scaffold,  a 
solution of 2 wt. in the first step. % of a natural polymer in distilled water was prepared by dissolving the polymer 
in the water and stirring the solution until the polymer was fully dissolved. It was also possible to prepare a 
solution of polyvinyl alcohol by dissolving PVA in distilled water at a temperature of 70 °C to prepare a solution

absorbance.

thermogravimetric  analyzer  (TGA-PL,  TGA  1500,  Canada)  was  employed  for  this  analysis,  conducted  in  a 
nitrogen atmosphere within the 25–600°C temperature range.

Investigation of scaffold biomineralization using simulated body fluid (SBF)
The performance of the scaffold bone graft was assessed using simulated body fluid (SBF), which was prepared 
following  established  protocols  with  chemical  reagents.  SBF  is  essential  for  examining  the  formation  of 
biomaterials on polymer scaffolds. To prepare the solution, 1000 mL of SBF was made by adding 700 mL of 
deionized water into a plastic container in a water bath. It is recommended to cover the container with either 
a glass or plastic lid while stirring; for the process to be successful, the solution should be kept at a consistent 
temperature of 36.5 °C throughout. Adding the ingredients in order is essential; once each ingredient is dissolved 
completely, the next one should be added, and so on. As soon as the ingredients were added, hydrochloric acid 
was used in the amount of 0–5 ml with an additive solution to achieve a pH of 7.4 in the resulting solution after 
adding the ingredients. A total of 1000 mL of solution was prepared by adding water to a flask and shaking it 
at 20 °C to reach the desired volume. The solution was then transferred to a polyethylene container and stored 
in a refrigerator at 5–10 °C. Scaffold samples were immersed in the SBF solution and incubated at 37 °C for 14 
days. After incubation, the samples were removed, rinsed with distilled water, and dried using the freeze-drying 
method. Finally, EDX and SEM techniques were employed to evaluate the biomineralization capability of the 
scaffold samples38.

for blood vessels and cell growth. Still, if there are many macropores in the scaffold, it will cause a noticeable 
drop in its mechanical properties. Therefore, choosing a scaffold with a suitable ratio of large and small pores is 
essential for bone tissue regeneration90. For bone defects, polymer scaffolds with a porosity higher than 80% are 
unsuitable91,92. According to the results shown in Fig. 7c–d, the porosity of the final PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF and

increases the hydrophobicity of the nanocomposite scaffold and, as a result, reduces the percentage of porosity94.
The control of the swelling behavior of the scaffolds, just like the control of the porosity parameter, is also 
of utmost importance if the scaffolds are to maintain their integrity in interaction with biological fluids. Thus, 
the swelling of the scaffolds can be attributed to the properties inherent in the constituent materials, which are 
responsible for causing the swelling. This allows control of swelling ability at the level of material selection11. 
The overall porosity and pore size are increased by swelling, resulting in the maximum possible surface area 
of the scaffold. When a sample shows a high degree of swelling, it can accept the maximum cell injection into 
the scaffold and create the maximum cell growth on the surface of the scaffold95. A proper interaction between 
the scaffold and the physiological fluid is essential for initial cell attachment, ultimately leading to better cell 
proliferation91.  As  shown  in  Fig.  7e–f,  the  most  swelling  was  obtained  in  CMC  scaffolds.  Considering  that

which  are  biodegradable,  and  is  derived  from  carbohydrate  sources76;  therefore,  due  to  its  very  hydrophilic

of scaffold swelling. In PVA/CMC scaffolds, negatively charged carbonyl groups (CH2COO-) from CMC and 
uncharged  carboxyl  groups  on  PVA  are  expected  to  contribute  to  the  hydrophilicity  of  the  scaffolds76.  The

Biodegradation measurements, and Thermogravimetric (TGA) analysis
The disintegration behavior of a scaffold is an essential factor in achieving a successful regeneration process, as 
it must match the rate of tissue formation. Scaffold samples must be stable enough to withstand regeneration67. 
Polyvinyl alcohol is a synthetic biodegradable polymer96. When composite scaffolds are soaked in PBS solution, 
they hydrolyze chemical bonds within them, causing weight loss due to the hydrolysis90. As a function of the 
time the scaffolds were submerged in PBS solution, the weight loss of the scaffolds was determined, as shown in 
Fig. 8a–b. As shown in this figure, in the first week, all scaffolds had a higher degradation rate, but after that, their 
degradation rate decreased. PBS medium reduces the weight of the scaffolds rapidly since physical and hydrogen 
bonds  mainly  connect  them.  HAp  synthesized  from  chicken  femur  is  crystalline,  as  shown  in  the  results  of 
SEM  analysis.  This  high  crystallization  of  HAp  can  reduce  its  degradation  kinetics,  and  therefore,  HAp  can 
help maintain the scaffold’s stability97. Adding HAp to the polymer scaffold containing polysaccharides reduces 
the buffer access to the sites of the polysaccharide molecules, which reduces the degradation of the scaffold88. 
Therefore,  scaffolds  made  of  different  biopolymers  containing  HAp  show  low  degradation11.  The  results  for 
the  PVA/CMC/HAp  scaffold  show  that  adding  HAp  has  reduced  the  degradation  rate  of  the  scaffold.  The 
ions released from HAp can reduce the rate of the degradation process and thus increase the bioactivity of the 
polymer scaffold98. Adding clay to the nanocomposite scaffold improves the degradation rate of the scaffold, and 
increasing the hydrophilicity of the scaffolds containing clay increases the diffusion of PBS inside the scaffolds 
and causes hydrolytic degradation20. Adding clay modified with Fe3O4 and GO reduces the degradation rate of 
the final scaffold. The clay plates form a strong interaction with the macromolecular chains of the biopolymer 
scaffold, which causes the hydrophilic groups to be consumed and the amount of solvent absorption to decrease, 
which protects the macromolecules from the hydrolysis process. Also, clay increases the stability of the polymer 
network67. Adding GO reduces the scaffold degradation rate92,99. The decrease in degradation of the polymer 
scaffold when adding GO is probably because GO sheets prevent the penetration of destructive substances in the 
phosphate buffer solution. In addition, the polymer matrix can have a more regular arrangement in the presence 
of GO, which is desirable for less penetration of destructive substances99. The increase of Fe3O4/GO reduces the 
degradation of the porous scaffold52. Alginate biopolymer has high biodegradability and is used as a drug and 
growth factor carrier13. Therefore, the PVA/Alg scaffold showed high biodegradability, which was reduced by 
adding HAp and CGF; however, for the final PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF nanocomposite scaffold, the biodegradation

Biomineralization of scaffolds in SBF analysis
As shown in Fig. 9a–f, after immersing the PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF and PVA/Alg/HAp and PVA/Alg nanocomposite 
scaffolds in SBF solution for 14 days, SEM images and EDX patterns were obtained. As it is clear from Fig. 9a–f, 
the hydroxyapatite layer is formed on the surface of scaffolds containing Alg and PVA. Following the immersion 
of the scaffold in SBF solution for 14 days, HAp is precipitated as unique spherical particles by accumulating high 
concentrations of Ca2+ and PO4
3- and forming on the surface of the scaffold108. Alginate as a biopolymer shows 
good  biomineralization;  adding  HAp  to  it  also  creates  an  organic–inorganic  compound,  similar  to  the  bone 
structure, which increases the biomineralization of the resulting scaffold109. By adding HAp to the raw materials 
of the scaffold, there is a noticeable increase in the formation of apatite crystals in the sample; according to the 
theory, this phenomenon occurs when Ca2+ ions are released from the scaffold structure and form an ionic bond 
with the SBF solution, which in turn leads to a more saturated concentration of Ca2+ ions and a higher pH value for 
the SBF solution, and as a result, apatite crystallization increases on the scaffold surface110. GO material facilitates 
spontaneous osteogenic differentiation and improvement of the biomineralization process23,111. The negatively 
charged carboxyl groups in GO interact with the Ca2+ cation in hydroxyapatite, thus facilitating hydroxyapatite 
formation. Also, scaffolds containing clay, using the nucleation site for hydroxyapatite deposition, show a high 
ability to induce the formation of hydroxyapatite because clay has a negative charge on its surface, which, like 
GO, can improve the hydroxyapatite precipitation on the surface of the scaffold67. As a result, according to the 
reasons explained, by adding CGF nanoparticles, the biomineralization of nanocomposite scaffolds increases.

this  causes  them  to  interact  with  the  calcium  ions,  which  have  a  positive  charge.  To  increase  the  adsorption

Cell viability and toxicity test in laboratory conditions
One of the important features of scaffolds designed for tissue engineering is biocompatibility, which indicates 
that they are non-toxic to cells for in vivo applications. A toxicity test called MTT was performed to examine the 
effect of biocompatibility proliferation and cell survival on the scaffolds. As a control sample, no scaffolds were 
used in the culture, and the toxicity test was performed in 72 h. The cell viability results in the scaffolds using 
the MTT toxicity test are shown in Fig. 12. When comparing the control sample to the existing scaffolds, it is 
evident that all the scaffolds exhibit greater cell viability than the control, suggesting that the prepared polymeric 
scaffolds are non-toxic. In addition to increasing mechanical properties, polymer composites can create a suitable 
environment for cell adhesion and growth. As shown in Fig. 12a, the PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF and PVA/CMC/HAp/
CGF nanocomposite scaffolds demonstrated the highest cell viability. This may be due to the added amount 
of Fe3O4 and GO to the polymeric matrix of the porous nanocomposite scaffold. Different functional groups 
of the polymeric matrix also increase cell survival due to more excellent cell adhesion. Hence, the synergistic 
effect of Fe3O4 and GO increases cell survival due to the cell compatibility nature of porous scaffolds44. One of 
the applications of GO in bone regeneration has been to construct a conductive bone scaffold to increase cell 
adhesion and provide a matrix for cell proliferation. The mechanical strength and tunable surface chemistry 
of GO have made it appear a promising platform for achieving the goal of cell proliferation116. Also, the CMC 
enhances the incorporation of hydrated media into the scaffolds to enhance cell adhesion without cytotoxicity76.
